templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Before + -ing), mid-sentence blank; the surgeon is the right subject
items.passage: In 1804, Japanese surgeon Hanaoka Seishū successfully removed a tumor from a patient under general anesthesia. Before attempting the procedure, ______ an herbal mixture, tsūsensan, that could induce a deep sleep lasting several hours.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: it took years of experiments for Hanaoka to develop
Hanaoka conducted years of experiments to develop
years of experiments by Hanaoka had gone into developing
Hanaoka’s years of experiments had gone into developing
items.explanation: The phrase “Before attempting the procedure” must describe the person who attempted it, so that person has to come right after the comma. Choice B places “Hanaoka” there, so the sentence clearly says that Hanaoka, before attempting the procedure, conducted years of experiments.

A.recipe: expletive opener (E), built on the experiments, not on the surgeon
A.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the opening phrase, so the sentence has no subject that could have attempted the operation; the phrase is left dangling.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “years of experiments,” so the sentence illogically says that the years attempted the procedure.

D.why_wrong: Hanaoka appears only in the possessive “Hanaoka’s”; the subject is “years of experiments,” which cannot attempt a procedure.

items.notes: Subject: Hanaoka Seishū’s 1804 operation under general anesthesia (history of medicine). Band 6 like 3.15 and 3.17: two sentences, a short prep + gerund opener (Before, not used in w2), clause-fragment options that run into the rest of the sentence. All four options share “years of experiments” and “develop”; the expletive is “it took ... for Hanaoka,” not an it-cleft of the key. Recipes E, W, P. Options 47 to 55 characters, key the shortest.

band7.why: Plain agent key (Hanaoka) with E, W and P distractors, the band-6 shape of dfbf5d33 and d2b81427; B and D both open with Hanaoka (plain and possessive), so the first word does not give the key; band_target 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Produced by ...), passage-final blank; the patterns (Chladni figures) are the right subject
items.passage: In 1787, German physicist and musician Ernst Chladni published a treatise demonstrating that the vibrations of a resonating object can be rendered visible as intricate geometric patterns. Produced by drawing a violin bow along the edge of a thin metal plate sprinkled with sand, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Chladni showed that the sand gathers along the lines where the plate is not vibrating.
the sand gathers into these patterns, now known as Chladni figures, along lines where the plate is not vibrating.
it is along the lines where the plate is not vibrating that the sand gathers into these patterns.
Chladni figures, as these patterns are now known, trace the lines where the plate is not vibrating.
items.explanation: What is produced by bowing a sand-covered plate is the pattern, so the patterns must be the subject that follows the comma. Choice D puts “Chladni figures, as these patterns are now known,” there, so the sentence says the figures are produced this way and trace the plate’s still lines.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the person
A.why_wrong: The subject is “Chladni,” so the sentence illogically says that the physicist himself was produced by drawing a bow along a plate.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the material one level off
B.why_wrong: The subject is “the sand,” but the sand is not produced by the bowing; the patterns it forms are.

C.recipe: expletive opener (E), a cleft built on “the lines”
C.why_wrong: The opening phrase is followed by “it,” which cannot be what the bowing produces, so the phrase is left dangling.

items.notes: Subject: Chladni figures, 1787 (science, acoustics). Band 6, passage-final full-sentence options like 772835db. The key’s subject begins with the scientist’s name used as a modifier (“Chladni figures”), while choice A begins with the scientist as a person, so a quick reader cannot pick by the first word; B keeps every fact with the sand, the concrete noun one level off. The cleft is built on “the lines,” not on the key’s subject. Options 86 to 111 characters, key not the longest.

band7.why: Plain-thing key (the patterns, named as Chladni figures) with W (the person, the sand) and E distractors, the band-6 shape of 772835db; A and D both open with “Chladni,” B keeps every fact with the sand, and the cleft C is built on “the lines,” not on the key; band_target 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head followed by a whose-clause with its own plural verb and three plural nouns; be-family options
items.passage: Each Thursday, Valencia’s Water Tribunal convenes outside the city’s cathedral to resolve disputes over irrigation. The authority of this court, whose members are elected by the farmers sharing the region’s eight canals, ______ rooted in centuries of tradition: hearings are conducted aloud in Valencian, and rulings cannot be appealed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “authority.” The phrase “of this court” and the clause “whose members are elected by the farmers sharing the region’s eight canals” only describe it, so the singular verb “is” is needed.

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the nearest nouns)
A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural; it agrees with the nearby plurals “farmers” and “canals,” not with the singular subject “authority.”

C.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “authority.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “authority.”

items.notes: Subject: the Water Tribunal of Valencia (social science, law and custom). Band-7 settings from dc645172 and 8a9d2f4e: head “authority” 15 words from the blank; the intervener carries its own plural finite verb (“are elected”) and three plural nouns (members, farmers, canals), with the plural “canals” right before the blank; 16 words of the run follow the blank. No possessive or pronoun after the blank points back to the head. Options: three plural forms, as the bank builds R1.

band7.why: Singular head (authority) 15 words from the blank behind a whose-clause with its own plural verb (are elected) and three plural attractors (members, farmers, canals), “canals” right before the blank, as 0fe5ce68 and 1c65db8f; 34-word run with 16 words after the blank; all three distractors plural, the 8a9d2f4e option set, so “are” sounds right twice.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural possessor before a singular head, then an appositive with a whose-clause carrying its own plural verb
items.passage: For nearly two centuries, Russian merchants traded grain for fish with Norwegians each summer along the Arctic coast. The two groups’ improvised language, a pidgin called Russenorsk, whose few hundred words derive mostly from Russian and Norwegian, ______ only in scattered word lists and transcribed dialogues.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The head of the subject is the singular noun “language”; the plural possessive “The two groups’” only says whose language it is, and the appositive “a pidgin called Russenorsk, whose few hundred words derive ...,” only describes it. The singular verb “survives” agrees with “language.”

B.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the possessor and the clause’s plural)
B.why_wrong: “Survive” is plural; it would suit “groups” or “words,” but the subject is the singular “language.”

C.why_wrong: “Have survived” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “language.”

D.why_wrong: “Are surviving” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “language.”

items.notes: Subject: Russenorsk, the Pomor trade pidgin (social science, linguistics). Band-7 settings from 863065c7 (possessor of the other number before the head) and f10b7ce4: plural possessor “groups’” before the singular head, then an appositive whose own clause has a plural verb (“derive”) agreeing with “words”; head to blank 14 words; the compound “Russian and Norwegian” right before the blank. Not the “among the ...” frame of w2b2_04 and w2b3_04.

fixes: added the comma before the nonrestrictive “whose few hundred words ...” (after the proper noun Russenorsk), passage and explanation

band7.why: Plural possessor (groups’) before the singular head as 863065c7, then a whose-clause with its own plural verb (derive) and the compound “Russian and Norwegian” right before the blank; 14 words head to blank. The singular appositive “a pidgin called Russenorsk” right after the head softens the possessor trap, but “words ... survive only in scattered word lists” is a natural garden path for the plural, which carries the item; all three distractors plural.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener (A pioneer of the genre ...), passage-final blank; the singer is the right subject
items.passage: Taarab, a form of sung poetry performed with an orchestra of string and percussion instruments, emerged at the royal court of Zanzibar in the late nineteenth century. A pioneer of the genre who began recording commercially in 1928, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Siti binti Saad’s performances in Swahili rather than Arabic helped the genre reach new audiences.
when Siti binti Saad performed in Swahili rather than Arabic, the genre reached new audiences.
Siti binti Saad helped the genre reach new audiences by performing in Swahili rather than Arabic.
the genre reached new audiences through Siti binti Saad’s performances in Swahili rather than Arabic.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “A pioneer of the genre who began recording commercially in 1928,” describes a person, so that person must be the subject that follows the comma. Choice C places “Siti binti Saad” there, so the sentence clearly says that she was the pioneer who helped taarab reach new audiences.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “performances,” so the sentence illogically says that performances were a pioneer who began recording in 1928.

B.why_wrong: The “when” clause comes right after the opening phrase, and the main clause’s subject is “the genre,” so the phrase describing a pioneer is left without the person it describes.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the genre,” so the sentence illogically says that taarab itself was a pioneer of the genre who began recording.

items.notes: Subject: Siti binti Saad and Zanzibari taarab (arts, music). Band 6, passage-final full-sentence options like a14eef71 and 2b6e1c06 (not the mid-sentence novel frame of 5b8f9cf2 and w2b3_05). All four options carry the same phrases (Siti binti Saad, in Swahili rather than Arabic, new audiences); recipes P, S, W; no expletive, so no cleft can mirror the key. Options 91 to 100 characters, key not the longest.

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (band7 appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on a14eef71 and 2b6e1c06: full-sentence options sharing every phrase, A and C both open with Siti binti Saad (possessive and plain), and the when-clause option (S) keeps her as a subject, only not of the main clause.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind singular nouns and a when-clause with its own singular verb; lexical-verb options
items.passage: The by-the-wind sailor (Velella velella), a blue relative of jellyfish, drifts across the open ocean propelled by a translucent sail. Mass strandings of the creature, triggered when a shift in the prevailing wind pushes its sail toward shore, ______ stretches of the Pacific coastline from Washington to California littered with millions of dried blue bodies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “strandings.” The phrase “of the creature” and the participial phrase “triggered when a shift in the prevailing wind pushes its sail toward shore” describe it, so the plural verb “leave” is needed.

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the nearest nouns and verb)
A.why_wrong: “Leaves” is singular; it matches the nearby “creature,” “shift,” “wind,” and “pushes,” not the plural subject “strandings.”

B.why_wrong: “Is leaving” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “strandings.”

C.why_wrong: “Has left” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “strandings.”

items.notes: Subject: by-the-wind sailors and their beach strandings (science, marine biology). Band-7 settings from 1c65db8f and b32eab9f: plural head behind five singular nouns (creature, shift, wind, sail, shore) and a when-clause whose own verb “pushes” is singular, so the wrong number sounds right twice; the singular “shore” right before the blank; head to blank 16 words, 15 run words after it.

band7.why: Plural head (strandings) behind five singular nouns (creature, shift, wind, sail, shore) and a when-clause with its own singular verb (pushes), as b32eab9f and 1c65db8f; 16 words head to blank, 34-word run with 15 words after the blank; all three distractors singular.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect (had already + participle) shared by a compound predicate, anchored by a later past event (when, in 1287, ...) 17 words after the blank
items.passage: Rabban Bar Sauma, a Christian monk born near present-day Beijing, ______ thousands of kilometers westward on a pilgrimage toward Jerusalem and resided for several years in Mongol-controlled Persia when, in 1287, its ruler appointed him ambassador to European monarchs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The journey and the years in Persia came before a later past event, the ruler’s appointment in 1287 (“when, in 1287, its ruler appointed him”). To show that one past action was finished before another, the past perfect is needed: “had already traveled,” whose “had” also carries “resided,” places both actions before that moment.

B.recipe: simple past where the past perfect is needed (as “already served” in 3.10)
B.why_wrong: “Already traveled” is past, but the simple past doesn’t show that the journey and the years in Persia were over before another past event, the appointment in 1287; that order calls for the past perfect.

C.recipe: present perfect where the past perfect is needed
C.why_wrong: “Has already traveled” ties the journey to the present, not to a time before the ruler appointed him in 1287.

D.recipe: past progressive where the past perfect is needed (as “was already serving” in 3.10)
D.why_wrong: “Was already traveling” presents the journey as still under way when he was appointed, but by 1287 it was over and he had been living in Persia for years.

items.notes: Subject: Rabban Bar Sauma’s 1287 embassy (history). The plan asks band 7, but no R4 item in CB’s bank is above band 5 and the template has no band-7 officials, so it is written as a strong band 6 (band_target 6), modelled on 3.10: blank right after the subject, the deciding “when, in 1287, ...” 17 words later, and a compound predicate (“and resided for several years”) the auxiliary must cover. Review: the set now follows 3.10 (simple past, past progressive, plus the present perfect); CB’s 3.10 rationale rejects the simple past in this exact frame.

fixes: all three distractors were present forms, each killed by the past “resided” alone (easier than its band-3 model 3.10); replaced “already travels” and “is already traveling” with 3.10’s lures “already traveled” (simple past) and “was already traveling” (past progressive), kept “has already traveled”; explanation, distractors and notes updated

band7.why: R4 has no CB item above band 5 and no band-7 officials, so it cannot be band 7, and band 6 is not reachable on CB evidence: the frame is 3.10 (d46ac7e7), filed hard but band 3. As written it was easier than 3.10 (three present-form distractors); with 3.10’s option set it is as hard as the rule allows. Future plans should move hard R4 cells to R1 or R2_interrupter (band7 doc, section 5).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head + gerund phrase and a comma interrupter full of plurals
items.passage: The tradition of cutting sculptures from discarded oil drums, now practiced in Croix-des-Bouquets, Haiti, by hundreds of artisans, ______ back to the 1950s, when Georges Liautaud, a blacksmith who forged crosses for cemeteries, began making freestanding figures.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “tradition”; “of cutting sculptures from discarded oil drums” and the phrase between the commas describe it. The singular verb “dates” agrees with “tradition.”

A.why_wrong: “Date” is plural; it agrees with the nearby “artisans” or “drums,” not with the singular subject “tradition.”

B.why_wrong: “Have dated” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “tradition.”

D.why_wrong: “Are dating” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “tradition.”

items.notes: Subject: Haitian oil-drum metal sculpture, Georges Liautaud (arts). Medium like 2.20: a comma interrupter between head and verb holding plural nouns, with “artisans” right before the blank. Nothing after the blank refers back to the head.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Without relying ...), mid-sentence blank; the plant is the right subject
items.passage: The squirting cucumber, a Mediterranean plant, disperses its seeds explosively. Without relying on the wind or animals, ______ up to several meters away.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the plant uses a jet of slimy liquid to fling its seeds
a jet of slimy liquid flings the plant’s seeds
the plant’s jet of slimy liquid flings its seeds
there is a jet of slimy liquid flinging the plant’s seeds
items.explanation: Only the plant can do without wind or animals to spread its seeds, so “the plant” must follow the opening phrase. Choice A does this, so the sentence says the plant, without relying on wind or animals, flings its seeds with a jet of liquid.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “a jet of slimy liquid,” so the sentence illogically says that the liquid avoids relying on wind or animals.

C.why_wrong: The plant appears only in the possessive “the plant’s”; the subject is “jet,” which is not what relies or doesn’t rely on wind.

D.why_wrong: “There” follows the opening phrase, so nothing in the main clause can be the thing that does without wind or animals.

items.notes: Subject: squirting cucumber seed ejection (science, botany). Medium like 2.2 and 2.17: short opener, mid-sentence blank, clause-fragment options. No option makes the seeds or the fruit the subject (seeds can sensibly “rely on wind,” which would make a second answer). Recipes W, P, E; key not the longest.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: plural possessor (fixed by “these”) + plain plural noun, two-slot grid
items.passage: Chaekgeori, folding screens that became fashionable among Korean scholars and officials in the late eighteenth century, depict bookshelves crowded with objects. Besides books, brushes, and inkstones, these ______ often hold porcelain vases, bronze vessels, and other luxury goods, some of them imported from Qing China.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The shelves belong to the screens, and “these” shows that there is more than one screen, so the plural possessive “screens’” is needed. “Shelves” is a plain plural that owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.why_wrong: “Screens” has no apostrophe, so it doesn’t show that the shelves belong to the screens.

B.why_wrong: “Screen’s” is a singular possessive, but “these” and the passage’s “folding screens” call for more than one screen.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Screens’” is right, but “shelves’” adds an apostrophe to a noun that doesn’t own anything in the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: chaekgeori bookshelf screens of late Joseon Korea (arts). Medium two-slot grid, the key a plural possessor (official medium R6 items use singular possessors; this varies the slot). “These” fixes the possessor’s number so “screen’s” cannot be read as a generic singular. Not the “Many of the ______” frame.

items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a dated event, framed by two dates (1577, 1580)
items.passage: In 1577, Ottoman astronomer Taqi al-Din finished building an observatory in Istanbul and filled it with instruments for charting the positions of stars and planets. The observatory ______ in use for only about three years, however: in 1580, Sultan Murad III, swayed by religious critics, ordered it torn down.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The observatory was finished in 1577 and torn down in 1580, so its time in use is a completed past event. The simple past “remained” fits, matching “finished” and “ordered.”

A.recipe: future where the past is needed
A.why_wrong: “Will remain” describes the future, but the observatory was used only between 1577 and 1580.

C.recipe: simple present where the past is needed
C.why_wrong: “Remains” describes the present, but the observatory was demolished in 1580.

D.recipe: present perfect next to a dated past
D.why_wrong: “Has remained” suggests the observatory is still in use, but it was torn down in 1580.

items.notes: Subject: Taqi al-Din’s Istanbul observatory (history of science). Medium like 2.12: dated past events on both sides of the blank. Past perfect is left out of the set so only one past form is offered.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: verb of a that-clause whose singular antecedent is in the main clause, interrupted by a reduced when-phrase with plural nouns
items.passage: Bladderworts, carnivorous water plants, catch prey with tiny underwater traps. Each trap is a hollow bladder sealed by a small door that, when brushed by passing water fleas or mosquito larvae, ______ open so quickly that the prey is sucked inside.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The relative pronoun “that” refers to “a small door,” which is singular, so the verb of the relative clause must be singular too. The plural nouns in “when brushed by passing water fleas or mosquito larvae” don’t change this: “swings” agrees with “door.”

A.why_wrong: “Swing” is plural; it agrees with “larvae” or “fleas,” not with “that,” which stands for the singular “door.”

B.why_wrong: “Have swung” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “door.”

D.why_wrong: “Are swinging” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “door.”

items.notes: Subject: bladderwort suction traps (science, botany). Medium: relative clause verb as in 2.18 and ee4aa2aa, with an interrupter between “that” and the blank so the plural “larvae” sits right before the blank.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a short subject
items.passage: Bird’s nest fungi produce cup-shaped fruiting bodies containing egg-like spore capsules called peridioles. When a raindrop strikes a cup, the impact ______ the peridioles up to a meter away.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause has a subject, “the impact,” but no verb. The finite verb “launches” supplies it.

A.recipe: -ing participle where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: “Launching” can’t serve as the main verb, so the clause after the comma has no verb.

B.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: “To launch” is not a finite verb, so the main clause lacks one.

C.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: “Having launched” is nonfinite and leaves the main clause without a verb.

items.notes: Subject: bird’s nest fungi (science, mycology). Easy: bare main-verb slot after a two-word subject; canonical four-form set. (Replaced parrotfish and then cave pearls, both claimed first by w2b5.)

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a plural subject
items.passage: Found in deserts from Egypt to Iran, yardangs are long, streamlined ridges that often resemble overturned boat hulls. Over thousands of years, sand-laden winds ______ them from soft rock.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence has a subject, “sand-laden winds,” but needs a main verb. The finite verb “carve” supplies it and agrees with the plural “winds.”

B.recipe: -ing participle where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: “Carving” can’t serve as the main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: “To carve” is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.

D.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: “Having carved” is nonfinite and leaves the sentence without a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: yardangs (science, geology). Easy: main verb right after its subject, plural key (as 1.31 and 1.23).

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: singular subject pronoun for “a ... shell”
items.passage: Female argonauts, small octopuses inhabiting the open ocean, secrete a thin, spiraled shell using two specialized arms. Unlike a snail’s shell, ______ is not attached to the animal’s body; instead, the female holds it in place with those same arms and deposits her eggs inside.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the argonaut’s shell, which is singular (“a thin, spiraled shell”). The singular pronoun “it” agrees with it and with the singular verb “is.”

A.why_wrong: “They” is plural, but the pronoun stands for the singular “shell.”

B.why_wrong: “These” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “shell.”

D.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “shell.”

items.notes: Subject: argonauts (paper nautiluses) and their egg-case shells (science, marine biology). Easy: antecedent in the previous sentence; the plural subject “argonauts” is there but the singular “is” after the blank and the meaning rule it out. Option set like 1.19 (pronoun plus demonstratives).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head + relative clause with a plural object; be-family options
items.passage: The Hispaniolan solenodon, a nocturnal mammal that feeds on insects and earthworms, ______ one of the few mammals capable of delivering venom through their teeth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “solenodon”; the appositive “a nocturnal mammal that feeds on insects and earthworms” only describes it. The singular verb “is” agrees.

A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural; it agrees with the nearby “earthworms,” not with the singular subject “solenodon.”

C.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “solenodon.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “solenodon.”

items.notes: Subject: Hispaniolan solenodon (science, zoology). Easy, one sentence like 1.40 (“one of the rare places”): a plain appositive between head and verb, with the plural “earthworms” right before the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head + appositive with plural nouns; lexical-verb options
items.passage: Michif, a language traditionally spoken by Métis communities in Canada and the northern United States, ______ French and Cree in an unusual way: its nouns are predominantly French, while its verbs are predominantly Cree.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “Michif”; the appositive “a language traditionally spoken by Métis communities ...” describes it. The singular verb “combines” agrees.

B.why_wrong: “Combine” is plural; it agrees with “communities,” not with the singular subject “Michif.”

C.why_wrong: “Are combining” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Michif.”

D.why_wrong: “Have combined” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Michif.”

items.notes: Subject: Michif, a French-Cree mixed language (social science, linguistics). Easy like 1.9: singular head, appositive containing a plural noun.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular name + participial phrase; lexical-verb options, compound predicate
items.passage: Jacques Roumain’s 1944 novel Masters of the Dew is set in a drought-stricken Haitian village. Manuel, back from years in Cuba’s sugarcane fields, ______ a hidden spring and encourages the feuding villagers to construct an irrigation canal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “Manuel,” one person, so the verb must be singular. “Finds” agrees with “Manuel” and matches the second verb, “encourages.”

A.why_wrong: “Find” is plural; it agrees with the nearby “fields,” not with the singular subject “Manuel.”

B.why_wrong: “Are finding” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Manuel.”

C.why_wrong: “Have found” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Manuel.”

items.notes: Subject: Jacques Roumain, Masters of the Dew (literature). Easy: a person named as subject with a short participial phrase between (as 1.20); not the “Its narrator, X, ______” frame of w2b2_18.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a recurring natural process (present-tense frame on both sides)
items.passage: Every autumn, spectators gather along the Qiantang River in eastern China to witness one of the world’s largest tidal bores. As the incoming tide is funneled into the river’s narrowing estuary, the water ______ into a single wave that propagates upstream against the current.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes something that happens every autumn, and the surrounding verbs are in the present (“gather,” “is funneled,” “propagates”). The simple present “piles up” fits this repeated event.

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Piled up” puts the event in the past, but it recurs every autumn and the other verbs are present.

B.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Had piled up” places the event before another past event, but the passage describes a present, recurring process.

D.recipe: future perfect where the present is needed
D.why_wrong: “Will have piled up” refers to a point in the future, which doesn’t fit a process described as happening every year.

items.notes: Subject: the Qiantang River tidal bore (science, earth science). Easy: habitual cue “Every autumn” plus present verbs in both clauses, as 1.17.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: singular possessive before a numeral, one slot
items.passage: Chinese writer Ba Jin’s 1931 novel Family portrays a wealthy household in Chengdu where a stern patriarch, Old Master Gao, demands total obedience. The ______ three young grandsons respond to his rule in very different ways, ranging from quiet submission to open rebellion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The grandsons belong to one patriarch, Old Master Gao, so the singular possessive “patriarch’s” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “Patriarchs” is a plain plural; it shows neither possession nor the single patriarch the passage names.

C.why_wrong: “Patriarchs’” is a plural possessive, but there is only one patriarch.

D.recipe: bare noun where a possessive is needed
D.why_wrong: “Patriarch” lacks the apostrophe and “s,” so it doesn’t show that the grandsons are his.

items.notes: Subject: Ba Jin, Family (literature). Easy single slot like 1.10 (“Moon’s”); the numeral after the blank rules out the bare noun used as a modifier. Not the “Many of the ______” frame.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: In Ilocos Norte, a province in the northern Philippines, many farmers belong to irrigation cooperatives called zanjeras. Each year, members reconstruct dams of bamboo and rock across rivers ______ water into their rice fields.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “members reconstruct dams of bamboo and rock across rivers” is already complete. The infinitive “to divert” adds the purpose of the work.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: “Diverted” would add a second past-tense verb with no conjunction joining it to “reconstruct.”

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: “Diverts” is a finite verb that doesn’t agree with “members” and leaves two main verbs with nothing joining them.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Is diverting” is a finite verb phrase that can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: zanjeras of Ilocos Norte (social science). Easy purpose infinitive like 1.27 and 1.22. Checked that “diverted” cannot read as a reduced relative on “rivers.”

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect in a counterfactual if-clause with “would/could have” in the main clause
items.passage: Dakota ethnographer Ella Deloria finished her novel Waterlily in the 1940s, but it remained unpublished until 1988, after her death. If the novel ______ during her lifetime, readers could have encountered its portrait of nineteenth-century Dakota family life decades sooner.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence imagines a past that did not happen, as “could have encountered” in the main clause shows. Such an if-clause takes the past perfect, “had been published.”

B.recipe: present where the past perfect is needed
B.why_wrong: “Is published” describes the present, but the condition concerns Deloria’s lifetime, which is past.

C.recipe: future where the past perfect is needed
C.why_wrong: “Will be published” describes the future, which can’t express an unreal past condition.

D.why_wrong: “Would have” belongs in the result clause (“could have encountered”), not in the if-clause.

items.notes: Subject: Ella Deloria’s Waterlily (literature). Easy counterfactual as in 1.15 (“If ... had reached ..., could have reacted”); the w2 R4_pastperf_future easy items so far used “earlier”/“before,” so this varies the cue.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: finite verb of a how-clause
items.passage: Published in 1637, Chinese scholar Song Yingxing’s encyclopedia Tiangong Kaiwu documents dozens of crafts and industries, from salt making to bronze casting. One chapter describes how papermakers ______ young bamboo stalks in water for several months before pounding them into pulp.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “how papermakers ______ young bamboo stalks” has a subject, “papermakers,” but needs a finite verb. “Soaked” supplies it.

A.recipe: -ing participle where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: “Soaking” is not finite, so the how-clause has no verb.

B.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: “To soak” is not finite, so the how-clause has no verb.

D.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: “Having soaked” is nonfinite and leaves the how-clause without a verb.

items.notes: Subject: Song Yingxing’s Tiangong Kaiwu on bamboo papermaking (history of technology). Easy like 1.14 (“recounts how his barbershop ______”), not the compound predicate of w2b3_23.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing participial phrase after a complete clause (pronoun + finite comma splices as distractors)
items.passage: The American dipper, a stocky gray songbird of western North America, forages underwater by walking along the beds of swift mountain streams. Gripping submerged rocks with its strong toes, it angles its body into the current, ______ the water’s pressure to hold itself against the streambed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “it angles its body into the current” is complete, so what follows the comma must be a phrase, not a second clause. The participle “using” begins a phrase that tells how the bird holds itself down.

A.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
A.why_wrong: “This uses” creates a second independent clause joined to the first only by a comma.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Uses” adds a second verb with no conjunction, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

D.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
D.why_wrong: “It uses” makes a second independent clause joined only by a comma.

items.notes: Subject: the American dipper walking underwater (science, ornithology). Easy, same option shape as 1.29 (-ing key against a bare finite form and two pronoun + finite splices).
